passages.title: The Preacher asks what work gains
passages.summary: The Preacher describes generations, wind, and rivers repeating their courses. He asks what lasting gain work brings. Vanity here concerns what does not last, not pride in appearance. Learning leaves the Preacher with more questions and grief.
passages.uncertainty: Jerusalem supplies the opening speaker’s setting.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies what gives temporary life lasting value. Why does the Preacher compare human work with wind and rivers?

passages.title: Pleasure and great works do not last
passages.summary: The Preacher builds houses, plants gardens, gathers wealth, and buys servants. He still finds no lasting gain. Someone else will inherit his work. He cannot control whether that person will use it wisely.
passages.uncertainty: Jerusalem supplies the opening speaker’s setting.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies mortal life as temporary. Why does leaving his work to another person trouble the Preacher?

passages.title: Changing times and shared death
passages.summary: The Preacher lists times for opposite actions. He describes injustice and asks what happens after death. People can enjoy their work without understanding all God does. Death also challenges claims of human superiority over animals.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies wisdom while recognizing life’s limits. Why does the Preacher connect enjoyment of work with what people cannot know?

passages.title: Power, lonely work, and companions
passages.summary: The Preacher sees people harmed without comfort. He compares a lonely worker with helpful companions. A companion can lift someone who falls. Endless work for wealth leaves the solitary worker asking whom he serves.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: What does a companion provide that the lonely worker’s wealth cannot?

passages.title: Listen before making promises
passages.summary: The Preacher warns against careless promises to God. He describes wealth that prevents sleep or disappears. A promise creates a duty to act. More possessions can bring more demands without bringing satisfaction.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Why does the Preacher prefer making no promise to leaving one unpaid?

passages.title: Having wealth without enjoying it
passages.summary: The Preacher describes a wealthy person unable to enjoy his goods. He asks who knows what is good. Long life and many children do not guarantee enjoyment. Another person can consume the goods the owner gathered.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: How does the wealthy person’s experience challenge measuring life by possessions?

passages.title: Mourning and unfair outcomes
passages.summary: The Preacher considers mourning, patience, and unfair outcomes. He also describes a woman as a trap. He sees good people die young and wrongdoers live long. These lives challenge simple rules about reward.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Why does the Preacher think a house of mourning can teach the living?

passages.title: A ruler’s power and delayed justice
passages.summary: The Preacher advises care before a king. He sees wrongdoers prosper and good people suffer. Delayed punishment can encourage further harm. His confidence in God stands beside outcomes he cannot explain.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: How does delayed punishment affect the people who watch wrongdoing?

passages.title: Death, chance, and forgotten wisdom
passages.summary: The Preacher urges enjoyment of food, work, and marriage. He recalls a poor man saving a city. The city forgets its poor rescuer. Wisdom can help without securing honor or lasting remembrance.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Why do the poor man’s useful words fail to bring him lasting honor?

passages.title: Small mistakes and careless rulers
passages.summary: The Preacher compares foolishness with flies spoiling perfume. He describes poor choices by rulers and workers. Sharpening an axe reduces wasted effort. Careful preparation matters more than using greater force.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: How does the blunt axe show the value of preparing before work?

passages.title: Act without knowing every outcome
passages.summary: The Preacher urges giving, sowing seed, and enjoying youth. He warns that people cannot predict every result. Waiting for perfect weather can prevent planting. Acting in several ways allows for outcomes the worker cannot foresee.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Scripture Helps connects bread on water with giving without expecting immediate repayment. Why does the Preacher tell the worker to sow in morning and evening?

passages.title: Remember your Creator before old age
passages.summary: The Preacher describes fading strength and death. The closing writer praises his teaching and urges obedience to God. The broken household images describe failing life. The closing writer turns from questions toward responsibility for hidden and public actions.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects lasting value with fearing God and keeping his commands. What does remembering the Creator change before the losses described in this chapter?
